beats.say: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. That is a linear pair. One of them is acute, and we want to know what kind the other must be.

board.text: Linear pair: one angle is acute. The other?

beats.say: First, the key fact. A straight line is a half turn, so the two angles of a linear pair always add up to 180 degrees.

board.text: Linear pair: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: Acute means small: less than 90 degrees. Let's try one. Say the acute angle is 50 degrees. How do we find its partner?

ask.ifNot: The two angles share 180 degrees between them. So the partner is whatever is left when we take 50 away from 180.

beats.say: 180 minus 50 is 130. That is more than 90 degrees, so the partner is an obtuse angle.
Was that just luck? Try an acute angle close to 90, say 80 degrees. Its partner is 180 minus 80, which is 100. Still more than 90.
Here is why it always works. 90 and 90 make 180. If one angle takes less than its 90, the other has to take more than 90 to make up the total.
So the other angle is always obtuse.
The trap is to say acute, because the two angles are a pair. But two acute angles together are less than 180, so they could never fill a straight line.
Remember it this way: on a straight line, a small angle always has a big partner.
We have three pairs of angles, and we are hunting for a supplementary pair. There may not be one at all.
First, what does supplementary mean? What must the two angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 90 degrees is for complementary angles. Supplementary angles fill a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So our test is simple. Add the pair. If the total is exactly 180, it is supplementary.

board.text: Supplementary: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: Pair A. 70 plus 20 is 90. That is a right angle, not a straight line. So A is out.
Pair B. 50 plus 50 is 100. Not 180 either.
Pair C looks tempting, because it has 180 in it. But we need the total to be 180. What is 100 plus 180?

ask.ifNot: Add the two angles together: 100, and 180 more. That goes well past 180.

beats.say: 280. Far too big. So C is out as well.
None of the three pairs adds up to 180. So the answer is: none of these.
It can feel odd to pick none of these. But we tested every pair, so we can be sure.
The method: for supplementary, add the pair and look for 180. Check every choice before you decide.
Three pairs of angles. One of them is a complementary pair, and we are going to find it.
What do complementary angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is for supplementary angles. Complementary angles fit together into one right angle, and a right angle is 90 degrees.

beats.say: So we add each pair and look for exactly 90.

board.text: Complementary: the two angles add up to 90°

beats.say: Pair A. 80 plus 20 is 100. Close, but 100 is not 90. A is out.
Pair B. 70 plus 110 is 180. That pair is supplementary, which is the other word. Easy to mix up! B is out.
Pair C. 50 plus 40. What do we get?

ask.ifNot: Add the tens: 5 tens and 4 tens make 9 tens.

beats.say: 90, exactly. So 50 degrees and 40 degrees are complementary.
A way to remember: C for complementary, C for corner. A corner is a right angle, 90 degrees.
So: add the pair. 90 means complementary, 180 means supplementary.
Two angles add up to 180 degrees. There is a special name for a pair like that.

board.text: Two angles add up to 180°. They are called ...?

beats.say: Here is a pair like that: 120 degrees and 60 degrees. Side by side they make a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.
Two names get mixed up all the time: complementary and supplementary. One goes with 90 degrees, the other with 180. Which is the name for 180?

ask.ifNot: Complementary goes with a corner, 90 degrees. The other word, supplementary, goes with a straight line, 180 degrees.

beats.say: Supplementary. Here is the trick: S for supplementary, S for straight line. And C for complementary, C for corner, which is 90 degrees.
What about the other two choices? Adjacent just means the angles are neighbours, sharing an arm. Their total can be anything.

board.text: Adjacent: next to each other, any total

beats.say: And vertically opposite angles face each other where two lines cross. They are equal, but they need not add up to 180.

board.text: Vertically opposite: across a crossing, equal

beats.say: So two angles with a sum of 180 degrees are called supplementary angles.
Whenever you see a total of 180, think straight line, think supplementary.
Two angles add up to 90 degrees. There is a special name for a pair like that.

board.text: Two angles add up to 90°. They are called ...?

beats.say: Here is a pair like that: 60 degrees and 30 degrees. Together they fill a square corner, and a square corner is a right angle, 90 degrees.
Two names get mixed up all the time: complementary and supplementary. One goes with 90 degrees, the other with 180. Which one goes with 90?

ask.ifNot: Supplementary goes with a straight line, 180 degrees. The other word, complementary, goes with a corner, 90 degrees.

beats.say: Complementary. Here is the trick: C for complementary, C for corner. And S for supplementary, S for straight line, which is 180 degrees.
What about the other two choices? Adjacent just means the angles are neighbours, sharing an arm. Their total can be anything.

board.text: Adjacent: next to each other, any total

beats.say: And vertically opposite angles face each other where two lines cross. They are equal, but they need not add up to 90.

board.text: Vertically opposite: across a crossing, equal

beats.say: So two angles with a sum of 90 degrees are called complementary angles.
Whenever you see a total of 90, think corner, think complementary.
Picture a compass. We want the angle between East and South.
A compass is a full circle. How many degrees are there in a full turn?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is only a half turn, a straight line. All the way round, back to where you started, is twice that.

beats.say: 360 degrees. And the 4 main directions, North, East, South and West, cut that circle into 4 equal parts.

board.text: N, E, S, W: 4 equal parts

beats.say: So each part is 360 divided by 4. That is 90 degrees, a quarter turn.
Now, East and South. Are they next-door neighbours on the compass, or is there another main direction between them?

ask.ifNot: Go round the compass in order: North, East, South, West. East and South come one straight after the other.

beats.say: They are neighbours. So turning from East to South is exactly 1 quarter turn.
The angle between East and South is 90 degrees. A right angle.
Check with the half-way direction, South-East. From East to South-East is 45 degrees, and from South-East to South is another 45. Together, 90.
So for the main compass directions, neighbours are always a quarter turn apart: 90 degrees.
Picture a compass. We want the angle between West and North-East.
North-East is one of the half-way directions. With those included, how many directions are there around the compass?

ask.ifNot: There are 4 main directions, and one half-way direction sits between each pair of them. That makes 4 more.

beats.say: 8 directions, equally spaced around a full turn of 360 degrees.

board.text: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW: 8 directions

beats.say: So each step from one direction to the next is 360 divided by 8, which is 45 degrees.
Now count the steps from West to North-East, the short way, over the top. West to North-West, then to North, then to North-East. How many steps?

ask.ifNot: Count the arrows, not the names. West to North-West is 1, North-West to North is 2, North to North-East is 3.

beats.say: 3 steps of 45 degrees. 3 times 45 is 135. The angle is 135 degrees.
Why the short way? Going round the other way is 5 steps, and 5 times 45 is 225. The angle between two directions is the smaller one.
And a check: 135 plus 225 makes 360, the full turn. The two ways round fit together.
The trap is to say 90, by treating North-East as if it were North. West to North is 90, and then there are 45 more.
So: 45 degrees for every step on the compass. Count the steps, then multiply.
We need the complementary angle of 37 and a half degrees.
Complementary angles are partners. What do the two partners add up to?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is for supplementary angles. Complementary angles fit into one right angle, a square corner, and that is 90 degrees.

beats.say: So our angle and its partner make 90 degrees together. To find the partner, we take 37 and a half away from 90.
Let's do it in two small steps. First the whole part: 90 minus 37 is 53.
Now there is still a half to take away. What is 53 minus a half?

ask.ifNot: Taking away a half makes the number smaller than 53, but not a whole 1 smaller. So it lands between 52 and 53.

beats.say: 52 and a half. So the complementary angle is 52 and a half degrees.
Check by adding the partners. 37 and 52 make 89. The two halves make 1 more. And 89 plus 1 is 90.
Watch out: if you take it away from 180 instead, you are finding the supplementary angle, which is a different partner.
So: complementary means the pair makes 90. Take the angle away from 90, whole part first, then the fraction.
We need the supplementary angle of 98 and a quarter degrees.
Supplementary angles are partners. What do the two partners add up to?

ask.ifNot: 90 degrees is for complementary angles. Supplementary angles fill a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So the partner is 180 take away 98 and a quarter.
Whole part first. From 98 up to 100 is 2, and from 100 up to 180 is 80. So 180 minus 98 is 82.
Now take a quarter from 82. Break 1 whole off the 82: that leaves 81 and 4 quarters. Take 1 quarter away from the 4 quarters. What is left?

ask.ifNot: We had 81 and 4 quarters. One quarter goes, so 3 quarters stay, and the 81 does not change.

beats.say: 81 and three quarters. So the supplementary angle is 81 and three quarters degrees.
Check by adding. 98 and 81 make 179. A quarter and three quarters make 1 whole. And 179 plus 1 is 180.
The slip to watch is 81 and a quarter. The quarter is being taken away, so it cannot just be copied into the answer.
So: supplementary means the pair makes 180. Take away the whole part first, then the fraction.
It is exactly 9 o'clock. We want the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand.

board.text: Angle between the hands at 9 o'clock = ?

beats.say: First, where are the two hands pointing at 9 o'clock?

choices: hour hand at 12, minute hand at 9
hour hand at 9, minute hand at 12
ask.ifNot: At an exact hour, the long minute hand points straight up at 12. The short hour hand points at the hour, which is 9.

beats.say: Now the clock face. It is a full circle, 360 degrees, and the 12 numbers cut it into 12 equal gaps.
So each gap, from one number to the next, is 360 divided by 12. That is 30 degrees.
Now count the gaps between the hands, the short way round. From 9 to 10, 10 to 11, 11 to 12. How many gaps?

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps, not the numbers. 9 to 10 is 1, 10 to 11 is 2, 11 to 12 is 3.

beats.say: 3 gaps of 30 degrees each. 3 times 30 is 90. The angle is 90 degrees.
Check it another way. 3 gaps out of 12 is a quarter of the clock, and a quarter of 360 is 90. The hands make a perfect square corner.
Don't go the long way round, from 12 all the way down to 9. That is 9 gaps. The angle between the hands is the smaller one.
So for any exact hour: count the gaps between the hands, and multiply by 30 degrees.
It is exactly 4 o'clock. We want the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand.

board.text: Angle between the hands at 4 o'clock = ?

beats.say: First, where are the two hands pointing at 4 o'clock?

choices: hour hand at 12, minute hand at 4
hour hand at 4, minute hand at 12
ask.ifNot: At an exact hour, the long minute hand points straight up at 12. The short hour hand points at the hour, which is 4.

beats.say: Now the clock face. It is a full circle, 360 degrees, and the 12 numbers cut it into 12 equal gaps.
So each gap, from one number to the next, is 360 divided by 12. That is 30 degrees.
Now count the gaps between the hands, the short way round. From 12 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4. How many gaps?

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps, not the numbers. 12 to 1 is 1, 1 to 2 is 2, 2 to 3 is 3, 3 to 4 is 4.

beats.say: 4 gaps of 30 degrees each. 4 times 30 is 120. The angle is 120 degrees.
Does that look right? At 3 o'clock the hands make a square corner, 90 degrees. At 4 o'clock they are 1 gap wider, and 90 plus 30 is 120.
The slip here is to count the numbers 12, 1, 2, 3, 4 and get 5. We count the gaps between them, and there are 4.
So for any exact hour: count the gaps between the hands, and multiply by 30 degrees.
Two angles are equal, and they are supplementary. We want the size of each one.
Supplementary tells us the total. What do supplementary angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 90 degrees is the total for complementary angles. Supplementary angles fill a straight line, which is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So the two angles add up to 180. They are equal, so let's call each one x.
x plus x is 2 lots of x. So 2 x equals 180.
2 times x is 180. How do we get x on its own?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 2, we divide by 2, and we do it to both sides.

beats.say: Divide both sides by 2. Half of 180 is 90. So x is 90.
Each angle is 90 degrees, a right angle. Check: 90 plus 90 is 180. Equal, and supplementary.
The trap is to share out 90 instead, which gives 45. But 90 is the total for complementary angles. Supplementary means 180.
So when two equal angles make a total, just halve the total.
Two complementary angles. One is x degrees and the other is x plus x degrees. We need to find x.
What do complementary angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is for supplementary angles. Complementary angles fit into a right angle, which is 90 degrees.

beats.say: So the first angle plus the second angle makes 90. Let's write that down.
Now count the x's on the left. How many are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every x you can see: one outside the bracket, and two inside it.

beats.say: 3 of them. So 3 x equals 90.
3 times x is 90, so we divide both sides by 3. 90 divided by 3 is 30.
Check. The first angle is 30. The second is 30 plus 30, which is 60. And 30 plus 60 is 90. Complementary!
The trap is to forget the first x and write 2 x equals 90. That gives 45, and then the angles would be 45 and 90. Far too much.
So: write the total as an equation, gather the x's, and divide.
Four pairs of angles. Three of them are supplementary, and one is not. We want the odd one out.
What do supplementary angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 90 degrees is for complementary angles. Supplementary angles fill a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So we add each pair, and look for the one that does not make 180.

board.text: Supplementary: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: Pair A. 70 plus 20 is 90. That is not 180. It looks like our odd one out, but let's check the others to be sure.
Pair B. 40 plus 140 is 180. Supplementary.
Pair C. 70 plus 110. What is the total?

ask.ifNot: Add the two angles carefully: start at 110, and count on 70 more.

beats.say: 180 again. And pair D: 120 plus 60 is 180 as well.
So only pair A does not make 180. 70 degrees and 20 degrees are not supplementary.
Notice the word not in the question. Three pairs pass the test here, and we want the one that does not.
70 and 20 make 90, so they are complementary instead. Add the pair: 90 is complementary, 180 is supplementary.
Two angles side by side on a straight line make a linear pair. This time one of them is obtuse. What kind is the other?

board.text: Linear pair: one angle is obtuse. The other?

beats.say: The key fact first. A straight line is a half turn, so the two angles of a linear pair always add up to 180 degrees.

board.text: Linear pair: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: Obtuse means wide: more than 90 degrees, but less than 180. Let's try one. Say the obtuse angle is 120 degrees. How do we find its partner?

ask.ifNot: Together the two angles make 180 degrees. So the partner is what is left when 120 is taken away from 180.

beats.say: 180 minus 120 is 60. That is less than 90 degrees, so the partner is an acute angle.
Try another, to be sure. An obtuse angle of 100 degrees leaves 180 minus 100, which is 80. Less than 90 again.
Here is why. 90 and 90 make 180. If one angle takes more than its 90, there is less than 90 left for the other.
So the other angle is always acute.
Don't be tempted by obtuse. Two obtuse angles would add up to more than 180, and that is too much for a straight line.
On a straight line, a big angle always has a small partner.
Two angles side by side on a straight line make a linear pair. One of them is 90 degrees. What kind of angle is the other?

board.text: Linear pair: one angle is 90°. The other?

beats.say: A straight line is a half turn. So the two angles of a linear pair always add up to 180 degrees.

board.text: Linear pair: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: One angle is 90. Which sum gives us the other one?

ask.ifNot: The two angles share 180 degrees. Take away the 90 we know, and what is left is the other angle.

beats.say: 180 minus 90 is 90. So the other angle is 90 degrees as well.
Now, what do we call an angle of exactly 90 degrees?

ask.ifNot: Acute is less than 90 degrees and obtuse is more than 90. Exactly 90 degrees, like the corner of your notebook, has its own name.

beats.say: A right angle. So the other angle is a right angle too.

board.text: The other angle is a right angle

beats.say: Check: 90 plus 90 is 180, a whole straight line. Picture a pole standing straight up on flat ground: a square corner on each side.
So for any linear pair, take the angle you know away from 180, then name what is left.
Picture a compass. We want the angle between North and West.
A compass is a full circle. How many degrees are there in a full turn?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is only a half turn, a straight line. All the way round, back to where you started, is twice that.

beats.say: 360 degrees. And the 4 main directions, North, East, South and West, cut that circle into 4 equal parts.

board.text: N, E, S, W: 4 equal parts

beats.say: So each part is 360 divided by 4. That is 90 degrees, a quarter turn.
Now, North and West. Are they next-door neighbours on the compass, or is there another main direction between them?

ask.ifNot: Go round the compass in order: North, East, South, West, and back to North. West and North come one straight after the other.

beats.say: They are neighbours. So turning from North to West is exactly 1 quarter turn.
The angle between North and West is 90 degrees. A right angle.
Check with the half-way direction, North-West. From North to North-West is 45 degrees, and from North-West to West is another 45. Together, 90.
So for the main compass directions, neighbours are always a quarter turn apart: 90 degrees.
An angle is bigger than 90 degrees but smaller than 180 degrees. What is it called?

board.text: An angle between 90° and 180° is called ...?

beats.say: Let's line up the angle names by size. The smallest kind is sharp and pointy, less than 90 degrees. That is an acute angle.
Exactly 90 degrees is the square corner, like the corner of your notebook. What is that one called?

ask.ifNot: A straight angle is a flat line, 180 degrees. The square corner, exactly 90 degrees, is the right angle.

beats.say: A right angle. And exactly 180 degrees is a flat, straight line, called a straight angle.
Our angle sits between those two. Wider than a square corner, but not yet flat. Like a book opened wide, or a hand fan.
Which name fills that gap?

ask.ifNot: Acute is the small, sharp one, under 90 degrees. Right is exactly 90. The wide one, between 90 and 180, has a different name.

beats.say: Obtuse. An angle between 90 degrees and 180 degrees is an obtuse angle.
A way to remember: acute is a cute little angle. Obtuse is the big, wide one.
So learn the two fence posts, 90 and 180. Below 90 is acute, and between them is obtuse.
Two angles add up to 140 degrees, and one of them is 85 degrees. We want the supplementary angle of the smaller one. That is two jobs.

board.text: Supplementary angle of the smaller one = ?

beats.say: First job: find the other angle. Which sum does that?

ask.ifNot: The two angles together make 140. We know one is 85, so the other is what is left of the 140.

beats.say: 140 minus 85. Take away 80 to get 60, then 5 more to get 55. The other angle is 55 degrees.
So the two angles are 85 degrees and 55 degrees. The smaller one is 55.
Second job: the supplementary angle of 55. What must 55 and its partner add up to?

ask.ifNot: 140 was the total of the first two angles, and that job is done. Supplementary partners always make a straight line, 180 degrees.

beats.say: So the partner is 180 minus 55. 180 minus 50 is 130, and 5 more off is 125.
Check: 55 plus 125 is 180. Yes, a straight line.
Two traps here. One is to stop at 55, which is only the first job. The other is to use the 85: that gives 95, the partner of the bigger angle.
For a two-job question, underline what is really being asked, and do the jobs one at a time.
Riya wants to cover a wall, 8 metres long and 5 metres wide, with rangoli paper. Each sheet covers exactly 4 square metres. How many sheets?

board.text: Wall 8 m × 5 m, 1 sheet covers 4 sq. m

beats.say: Each sheet covers an area. So what do we need to know about the wall first?

ask.ifNot: Paper covers a surface: the flat space inside the edges. That space is the wall's area.

beats.say: Area is length times breadth. 8 times 5 is 40 square metres.
Each sheet covers 4 of those 40 square metres. How do we find the number of sheets?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many 4s fit into 40. That is a division.

beats.say: 40 divided by 4 is 10. Riya needs 10 sheets.
Check: 10 sheets of 4 square metres each. 10 times 4 is 40. The whole wall is covered.
The slip is to stop at 40. That is the wall's area in square metres, not the number of sheets. And 13 is just 8 plus 5, which is not an area at all.
Covering questions go like this: area of the whole thing, divided by the area 1 piece covers.
Ravi's kitchen floor is 9 metres long and 7 metres wide. In the middle is a square pillar of side 1.5 metres. Each tile covers 0.25 square metres. How many tiles for the rest of the floor?

board.text: Kitchen 9 m × 7 m, square pillar of side 1.5 m
Each tile covers 0.25 sq. m. How many tiles?

beats.say: Two jobs. First find the area that needs tiles: the floor, take away the pillar. Then see how many tiles fill it.
The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the floor, 9 times 7 is 63 square metres.
Now the pillar. It is a square, so side times side: 1.5 times 1.5. 1 times 1.5 is 1.5, and half of 1.5 is 0.75. Together, 2.25 square metres.
Take the pillar away from the floor. 63 minus 2 is 61, and 0.25 more off leaves 60.75 square metres.
Each tile covers 0.25 of a square metre. That is a quarter. So how many tiles cover 1 whole square metre?

ask.ifNot: 0.25 is one quarter, and 4 quarters make a whole. So 4 tiles cover 1 square metre.

beats.say: 4 tiles for every square metre. So we need 60.75 times 4. 60 times 4 is 240, and 0.75 times 4 is 3. That makes 243 tiles.
Check: 243 tiles, each a quarter of a square metre, cover 243 divided by 4, which is 60.75. Just right.
If you forget the pillar, you get 63 times 4, which is 252 tiles. 9 of those would have nowhere to go.
So: area to cover, divided by the area of 1 tile. Dividing by a quarter is the same as multiplying by 4.
Vikram's courtyard is a square with an area of 625 square metres. A path 2 metres wide goes all round the outside. We want the area of the path alone.

board.text: Path 2 m wide all round, outside. Path area = ?

beats.say: We need the side of the courtyard first. A square's area is side times side, and 20 times 20 is only 400. So which number, times itself, makes 625?

ask.ifNot: Halving 625, or sharing it by 4, does not undo side times side. We need a number times itself, a bit bigger than 20.

beats.say: It is 25. Let's make sure: 25 times 20 is 500, and 25 times 5 is 125. Together, 625. So the courtyard is 25 metres on each side.
Now add the path, 2 metres wide, all the way round. How long is one side of the big outer square?

ask.ifNot: The path sticks out 2 metres on one side, and 2 metres on the opposite side as well. So the side grows by 4 metres.

beats.say: 25 plus 2 plus 2 is 29. The outer square, courtyard and path together, is 29 metres on each side.
Its area is 29 times 29. A quick way: 29 times 30 is 870, then take away one 29. That leaves 841 square metres.
The path is the outer square with the courtyard taken out. 841 minus 625 is 216 square metres.
A tempting shortcut gives 200: the distance round the courtyard, 100 metres, times 2. But that misses the 4 corner squares of the path, each 2 by 2. They add 16, which makes 216.
For a path round the outside: outer area minus inner area. And the side grows by twice the width of the path.
Ravi's garden is 18 metres long and 12 metres wide. A path 2 metres wide runs all the way round, just inside the edge. The vegetable patch is what is left in the middle.

board.text: Garden 18 m × 12 m, path 2 m wide inside

beats.say: The patch is a smaller rectangle. The path is 2 metres wide. So how much shorter than the garden is the patch?

ask.ifNot: The path runs along both ends of the garden. It takes 2 metres off one end and 2 metres off the other end. That is 4 metres altogether.

beats.say: So the length of the patch is 18, take away 2, take away 2 again. That is 14 metres.
The width loses 2 metres on each side as well. 12, take away 2, take away 2, is 8 metres.
Now the patch is a rectangle, 14 by 8, and area is length times breadth. 10 times 8 is 80, and 4 times 8 is 32. Together, 112 square metres.
Check against the whole garden. 18 times 12 is 216 square metres. The patch takes 112, leaving 104 for the path. A patch smaller than the garden: sensible.
The classic slip is to take the path off only once. That gives 16 by 10, which is 160: much too big. A path all the way round comes off twice.
For a border inside a rectangle: take twice its width off the length, and twice off the breadth, then multiply.
Aarav is tiling a kitchen floor that is 12 metres long and 9 metres wide. Each square tile has a side of 3 metres. How many tiles does he need?

board.text: Floor 12 m × 9 m, square tiles of side 3 m

beats.say: To cover a floor we need its area. Length times breadth: 12 times 9 is 108 square metres.
Now the tile. It is a square with a side of 3 metres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9. So each tile covers 9 square metres.
The floor is 108 square metres and each tile covers 9. How do we find the number of tiles?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many tile areas fit into the floor area. So we divide area by area: 108 by 9, not by the side of the tile.

beats.say: 108 divided by 9. We know that 9 times 12 is 108, so the answer is 12. Aarav needs 12 tiles.
Check by picturing the tiles. 4 fit along the length, and 3 rows fit down the breadth. 4 times 3 is 12.
The trap is to divide 108 by 3, the side of the tile. That gives 36, three times too many. A tile covers an area, so divide by its area.
For tiling: floor area, divided by the area of 1 tile.
Priya's courtyard is 12 metres long and 8 metres wide. A rangoli border 1 metre wide runs all round the inside edge. We want the area of just the border.

board.text: Courtyard 12 m × 8 m, border 1 m wide inside

beats.say: A border is a frame shape, awkward to measure directly. So here is the trick: find the whole courtyard, find the empty middle, and subtract.
The whole courtyard first. 12 times 8 is 96 square metres.
Now the inner rectangle. The border is 1 metre wide. How long is the inner rectangle?

ask.ifNot: The border runs along both ends. It takes 1 metre off one end and 1 metre off the other, so the length loses 2 metres.

beats.say: 12, take away 1, take away 1, is 10. In the same way the width is 8, take away 1, take away 1, which is 6.
So the inner rectangle is 10 by 6. Its area is 60 square metres.
The border is the difference. 96 minus 60 is 36 square metres.
Careful: 60 is one of the choices, but that is the middle, not the border. The question asks for the frame around it.
Another tempting shortcut is distance round times width: 40 times 1 is 40. But that counts each of the 4 corner squares twice. Take 4 off, and we get 36 again.
For the area of a border: outer rectangle, minus inner rectangle.
Riya's bedroom is 12 metres long and 9 metres wide. A carpet, 8 metres by 5 metres, lies in the centre. The rest of the floor gets square tiles of side 50 centimetres. How many tiles?

board.text: Room 12 m × 9 m, carpet 8 m × 5 m
Square tiles of side 50 cm. How many?

beats.say: Which part of the floor gets tiles?

ask.ifNot: Tiles go on the bare floor, not under the carpet. So the carpet's area comes off the room's area.

beats.say: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the room, 12 times 9 is 108 square metres.
Now the carpet. 8 times 5 is 40, so it covers 40 square metres.
Now take the carpet away from the room. 108 minus 40 is 68 square metres.
Now the tiles. Careful: the room is measured in metres, but the tile is in centimetres. 50 centimetres is half a metre, so 2 tiles fit along 1 metre.
So how many tiles cover 1 whole square metre?

ask.ifNot: 2 tiles fit along the metre, and 2 rows fit down it. 2 rows of 2 makes 4 tiles.

beats.say: 4 tiles for each square metre, and there are 68 square metres. 60 times 4 is 240, and 8 times 4 is 32. That makes 272 tiles.
Two slips to watch. Saying 2 tiles for a square metre forgets the second row. And tiling under the carpet gives 108 times 4, which is 432.
So: make the units match, find how many tiles fill 1 square metre, then multiply by the area.
Riya's floor is 12 metres long and 8 metres wide. A square rangoli mat of side 3 metres lies in the centre. She paints the rest, and 1 can of paint covers 15 square metres. How many cans?

board.text: Floor 12 m × 8 m, square mat of side 3 m
1 can covers 15 sq. m. How many cans?

beats.say: Before we can count cans, we need the area that gets painted: the floor, take away the mat.
The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the floor, 12 times 8 is 96 square metres.
Now the mat. It is a square with a side of 3 metres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9. So the mat covers 9 square metres.
Now take the mat away from the floor. 96 minus 9 is 87 square metres.
Now the cans. Each one covers 15 square metres. Let's count up: 5 cans cover 75, and 6 cans cover 90.
Riya has 87 square metres to paint. How many cans must she buy?

ask.ifNot: 5 cans reach only 75 square metres, so 12 square metres of floor would stay bare. She cannot buy part of a can, so she needs the next whole can.

beats.say: 6 cans. The sixth can will only be partly used, but she still has to buy it.
That is the trap in this question. 87 divided by 15 is 5 and a bit, and it is tempting to say 5. When you are buying whole cans, a bit over means 1 more can.
So: find the area, divide by what 1 can covers, and round up if there is anything left over.
Ankit's kitchen floor is 9 metres long and 5 metres wide. Each square tile has a side of 1 metre and costs 45 rupees. What will all the tiles cost?

board.text: Floor 9 m × 5 m, tiles of side 1 m, ₹45 each

beats.say: Each tile is 1 metre by 1 metre, so it covers exactly 1 square metre. That means the number of tiles is the same as the floor's area. Which sum gives that?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides only counts along the edges. Tiles fill the whole floor, row after row: 5 rows of 9.

beats.say: 9 times 5 is 45. The floor is 45 square metres, so it takes 45 tiles.
Now the cost. 45 tiles, at 45 rupees each. Careful: the two 45s are different things. One counts tiles, the other counts rupees.
How do we find the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 45 tiles costs 45 rupees. 45 lots of 45 is a multiplication.

beats.say: Split one 45 into 40 and 5. 45 times 40 is 1,800, and 45 times 5 is 225. Together, 2,025 rupees.
Does that feel right? 45 is a little less than 50, and 45 times 50 would be 2,250. A little less than 2,250 is sensible.
The choices 630 and 1,260 come from adding the sides, or going round the edge, to count the tiles. Tiles cover the inside of the floor, so we need the area.
So: area gives the number of tiles, and tiles times price gives the cost.
Arjun has 120 metres of rope to go round a rectangular cover. The length is twice the breadth. Then a square hole of side 5 metres is cut in the middle. We want the area that is left.

board.text: Square hole of side 5 m. Area left = ?

beats.say: We don't know the sides yet, so think in parts. Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length, which is twice as long, is 2 parts.
The rope goes all the way round: a length, a breadth, another length, another breadth. How many parts is that altogether?

ask.ifNot: Going round a rectangle, we pass 2 lengths and 2 breadths. That is 2 parts, and 1, and 2, and 1.

beats.say: 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6 parts. Those 6 parts use all 120 metres of rope, so 1 part is 120 divided by 6, which is 20 metres.
So the breadth is 20 metres, and the length is twice that, 40 metres. Check the rope: 40 plus 20 plus 40 plus 20 is 120.
Now the area of the whole cover. 40 times 20 is 800 square metres.
Now the hole. It is a square with a side of 5 metres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 5 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 5 times 5 is 25. Take the hole out of the cover: 800 minus 25 is 775 square metres.
The big trap is sharing the 120 metres by 3, as if the rope were just 1 length and 1 breadth. That gives a breadth of 40, and a cover far too big. A perimeter has 2 of each.
So: use the perimeter to find the sides, then the area, then take away the hole.
Priya's kitchen floor is 8 metres by 6 metres, with a square pillar of side 1 metre in the centre. The rest gets square tiles of side 25 centimetres, at 12 rupees a tile. What is the cost?

board.text: Floor 8 m × 6 m, square pillar of side 1 m
Tiles of side 25 cm, ₹12 each. Cost = ?

beats.say: There are three jobs here: the area to tile, the number of tiles, and the cost. Which one has to come first?

ask.ifNot: We cannot price the tiles until we have counted them, and we cannot count them until we know how much floor they cover. So the area comes first.

beats.say: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the floor, 8 times 6 is 48 square metres.
The pillar is a square of side 1, so its area is 1 times 1, which is just 1 square metre.
Now take the pillar away from the floor. 48 minus 1 is 47 square metres.
Now the tiles. Each is 25 centimetres wide, and 4 of them make 100 centimetres, which is 1 metre. So 4 tiles fit along a metre.
How many tiles cover 1 whole square metre?

ask.ifNot: 4 tiles fit along the metre, and 4 rows fit down it. 4 rows of 4 makes 16.

beats.say: 16 tiles for each square metre, and 47 square metres. 47 times 10 is 470, and 47 times 6 is 282. Together, 752 tiles.
Last job, the cost. 752 tiles at 12 rupees each. 752 times 10 is 7,520, and 752 times 2 is 1,504. Together, 9,024 rupees.
If you forget the pillar, 48 times 16 is 768 tiles, and the bill comes to 9,216. That is one of the choices, so take care.
A long question is just short jobs in a row: area, then tiles, then cost. Finish one before starting the next.
A large square rangoli has a side of 20 centimetres. A smaller square, of side 12 centimetres, sits in the middle. Coloured powder fills the space between them.

board.text: Large square of side 20 cm, small square of side 12 cm

beats.say: The powder goes between the two squares. So we want the area of the large square, take away the area of the small one.
The area of a square is side times side. For the large square, 20 times 20 is 400 square centimetres.
Now the small square. It is a square with a side of 12 centimetres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 12 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 12 times 12 is 144. So the small square covers 144 square centimetres.
Now take the small square away from the large one. 400 minus 100 is 300, and 300 minus 44 is 256 square centimetres.
Check by adding back. 256 plus 144 is 400, the large square.
A tempting shortcut is to subtract the sides first: 20 minus 12 is 8, and 8 times 8 is 64. That is far too small. Find each area, then subtract.
So for a shape inside a shape: big area, minus small area.
Priya's courtyard is a square of side 20 metres. She leaves a border 2 metres wide all round, and fills the inside with coloured powder that costs 15 rupees for each square metre.

board.text: Square courtyard of side 20 m, border 2 m wide

beats.say: The rangoli fills the inner square. The border is 2 metres wide. How long is one side of that inner square?

ask.ifNot: The border runs down both edges. It takes 2 metres off one side and 2 metres off the opposite side, so 4 metres go.

beats.say: 20, take away 2, take away 2, is 16. The inner square is 16 metres on each side.
Its area is side times side. 16 times 10 is 160, and 16 times 6 is 96. Together, 256 square metres.
Each square metre of powder costs 15 rupees. How do we find the cost of 256 square metres?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 256 square metres costs 15 rupees. 256 lots of 15 is a multiplication.

beats.say: 15 is 10 and 5. 256 times 10 is 2,560. 256 times 5 is half of that, 1,280. Together, 3,840 rupees.
Two traps. Pricing the whole courtyard, 400 square metres, gives 6,000. And taking the border off only one way gives 20 times 16, which is 320, and a cost of 4,800.
A border all round comes off twice from each side. Then find the area, then the cost.
Ananya's courtyard is 18 metres long and 12 metres wide. A diagonal cuts it into two equal triangles, and she paints one. Then a square flower bed of side 4 metres goes inside the painted triangle.

board.text: Courtyard 18 m × 12 m, cut by a diagonal
One triangle painted, with a square bed of side 4 m

beats.say: Start with the whole courtyard. Length times breadth: 18 times 10 is 180, and 18 times 2 is 36. Together, 216 square metres.
The diagonal cuts the rectangle into two equal triangles. So how do we find the area of one triangle?

ask.ifNot: Two equal triangles share the rectangle between them. So each one gets half of the 216.

beats.say: Half of 216 is 108. The painted triangle is 108 square metres.
Now the flower bed. It is a square of side 4, so its area is 4 times 4, which is 16 square metres.
The bed covers up 16 of the painted square metres. Take it away: 108 minus 16 is 92 square metres.
Check by adding back. 92 plus 16 is 108, the whole painted triangle.
Two slips. 108 is the triangle before the flower bed goes in. And 200 comes from taking the bed away from the whole courtyard, forgetting that only half was painted.
Go in the order of the story: the whole rectangle, half of it, then take away the piece on top.
Rohan's bathroom floor is a square with a side of 50 centimetres. He covers it with small square tiles of side 5 centimetres. How many tiles?

board.text: Square floor of side 50 cm, square tiles of side 5 cm

beats.say: Tiles cover a surface, so we need areas. The floor is a square, so its area is side times side: 50 times 50 is 2,500 square centimetres.
Now the tile. It is a square with a side of 5 centimetres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 5 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 5 times 5 is 25. So each tile covers 25 square centimetres.
The floor is 2,500 square centimetres and each tile covers 25. How do we find the number of tiles?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many tile areas fit into the floor area. So we divide area by area: 2,500 by 25, not by the side of the tile.

beats.say: 25 times 100 is 2,500. So 2,500 divided by 25 is 100. Rohan needs 100 tiles.
Check by picturing the tiles. 50 divided by 5 is 10, so 10 tiles fit in a row. And there are 10 rows. 10 times 10 is 100.
That shows the trap. 10 is only the number of tiles along 1 edge. The floor needs row after row of them.
For tiling: floor area, divided by the area of 1 tile.
Meera's card is 24 centimetres long and 18 centimetres wide. A square photo of side 10 centimetres is pasted in the centre. Glitter paint for the rest costs 2 rupees for each square centimetre.

board.text: Card 24 cm × 18 cm, square photo of side 10 cm
Glitter paint: ₹2 per sq. cm. Cost = ?

beats.say: Before any cost, we need an area. Which area gets glitter paint?

ask.ifNot: No glitter goes on the photo. So the photo's area has to come off the card's area.

beats.say: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the card: split the 18 into 10 and 8. 24 times 10 is 240, and 24 times 8 is 192. Together, 432.
So the card has an area of 432 square centimetres.
Now the photo. It is a square, so its area is side times side: 10 times 10 is 100 square centimetres.
Now take the photo away from the card. 432 minus 100 is 332 square centimetres.
Each square centimetre costs 2 rupees. How do we find the cost of 332 square centimetres?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 332 square centimetres costs 2 rupees. 332 lots of 2 is a multiplication.

beats.say: 332 times 2 is 664. Meera spends 664 rupees.
If you forget the photo, you get 432 times 2, which is 864. But no glitter goes on the photo.
So: the area that is really painted, times the price of 1 square centimetre.
Riya's room is 12 metres long and 8 metres wide, with a square rangoli of side 3 metres in one corner. The rest of the floor gets small square tiles of side 50 centimetres. How many tiles?

board.text: Room 12 m × 8 m, square rangoli of side 3 m
Square tiles of side 50 cm. How many?

beats.say: Two jobs. First the area to tile: the room, take away the rangoli. Then count how many tiles fill it.
The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the room, 12 times 8 is 96 square metres.
Now the rangoli. It is a square with a side of 3 metres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9. So the rangoli covers 9 square metres.
Now take the rangoli away from the room. 96 minus 9 is 87 square metres.
Now one tile. Its side is 50 centimetres, which is 0.5 of a metre. So its area is 0.5 times 0.5. What is that?

ask.ifNot: Half of a half is a quarter. And a quarter, written as a decimal, is 0.25.

beats.say: 0.25 of a square metre, a quarter. So 4 tiles cover 1 whole square metre.
87 square metres, with 4 tiles in each. 80 times 4 is 320, and 7 times 4 is 28. That makes 348 tiles.
The big trap is the units. If you divide 87 by 50, you are mixing metres with centimetres. Always change the tile into metres first.
And remember the rangoli. Without taking it away you would get 96 times 4, which is 384.
So: area to tile, in square metres, times the number of tiles in 1 square metre.
Ananya's garden is a triangle. The distance round it is 72 metres, and its sides are in the ratio 3 to 4 to 5. We want its area.

board.text: Triangle: perimeter 72 m, sides in ratio 3 : 4 : 5

beats.say: A ratio is about equal parts. The sides are 3 parts, 4 parts and 5 parts. How many parts make up the whole 72 metres?

ask.ifNot: The 72 metres is all three sides put together. So we add the parts: 3 and 4 and 5.

beats.say: 3 plus 4 plus 5 is 12 parts. So 1 part is 72 divided by 12, which is 6 metres.
Now the sides. 3 parts is 18 metres, 4 parts is 24 metres, and 5 parts is 30 metres.
The question hints that this triangle is special. Test it: 18 times 18 is 324, and 24 times 24 is 576. Together, 900. And 30 times 30 is 900 as well.
When the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side, the triangle has a right angle. So 18 and 24 meet at a square corner: they are the base and the height.
So which sum gives the area of this right-angled triangle?

ask.ifNot: A right-angled triangle is half of a rectangle, so we must halve. And we use the two sides that meet at the right angle, 18 and 24, not the slanted side.

beats.say: 18 times 20 is 360, and 18 times 4 is 72, so 18 times 24 is 432. Half of 432 is 216 square metres.
A quick check on the sides: 18 plus 24 plus 30 is 72, the perimeter we were given.
So: share the perimeter by the ratio to get the sides, spot the right angle, then take half of base times height. The answer is 216 square metres.
Arjun's triangle has sides of 9, 12 and 15 centimetres. Meena doubles every side. By how much does the area go up?

board.text: Every side doubled. Increase in area = ?

beats.say: First, what kind of triangle is it? Test for a right angle. 9 times 9 is 81, 12 times 12 is 144, and together they make 225. And 15 times 15 is 225 too.
They match, so it is a right-angled triangle. The two shorter sides, 9 and 12, meet at the right angle. They are the base and the height.
The area is half of base times height. 9 times 12 is 108, and half of 108 is 54 square centimetres.
Now double every side. The new triangle is 18, 24 and 30. Its base is 18 and its height is 24.
Before we work it out, have a guess. When every side is doubled, what happens to the area?

ask.ifNot: It is natural to say it doubles. But the base doubles and the height doubles too, so the area is doubled twice. Let's work it out and see.

beats.say: 18 times 20 is 360, and 18 times 4 is 72, so 18 times 24 is 432. Half of 432 is 216 square centimetres.
216 is 4 times 54. But the question asks for the increase: 216 minus 54 is 162 square centimetres.
Three traps in the choices. 54 is the old area, 216 is the new area, and 108 comes from thinking the area only doubles. The increase is the gap between new and old.
Double every side and the area becomes 4 times as big. So the increase is 3 times the old area: 3 times 54 is 162.
Arjun's kitchen floor is 9 metres long and 7 metres wide. A square pillar of side 1.5 metres takes up one corner. Tiles for the rest cost 120 rupees for each square metre.

board.text: Kitchen 9 m × 7 m, square pillar of side 1.5 m

beats.say: Before the cost, we need an area. Which area needs tiles?

ask.ifNot: Tiles cannot go where the pillar stands. So the pillar's area comes off the floor's area.

beats.say: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the floor, 9 times 7 is 63 square metres.
Now the pillar. It is a square, so side times side: 1.5 times 1.5. 1 times 1.5 is 1.5, and half of 1.5 is 0.75. Together, 2.25 square metres.
Take the pillar away from the floor. 63 minus 2 is 61, and 0.25 more off leaves 60.75 square metres.
Each square metre costs 120 rupees. How do we find the cost of 60.75 square metres?

ask.ifNot: We pay 120 rupees for every square metre, and there are 60.75 of them. So many lots of 120 is a multiplication.

beats.say: Split the 120 into 100 and 20. 60.75 times 100 is 6,075, and 60.75 times 20 is 1,215. Together, 7,290 rupees.
Forget the pillar and you get 63 times 120, which is 7,560. That is one of the choices. But tiles do not go under a pillar.
So: the area that really gets tiles, times the price of 1 square metre.
Arjun is painting a wall that is 8 metres long and 5 metres tall. In the middle is a square window with a side of 2 metres, which he does not paint.

board.text: Wall 8 m × 5 m, square window of side 2 m

beats.say: Arjun paints the wall but not the window. So the area to paint is the wall's area, take away the window's area.
The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the wall, 8 times 5 is 40 square metres.
Now the window. It is a square with a side of 2 metres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 2 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 2 times 2 is 4. So the window covers 4 square metres.
Now take the window away from the wall. 40 minus 4 is 36 square metres.
Check by adding back. 36 plus 4 is 40, the whole wall.
The slip to watch is taking away 2, the side of the window, and not 4, its area. And never add the window on: that would give 44.
So: area of the wall, minus the area of the window.
Vikram is painting a wall, 10 metres long and 4 metres high. It has two square windows, each of side 1.5 metres, and a door 2 metres wide and 3 metres tall. He paints only the wall itself.

board.text: 2 square windows of side 1.5 m, door 2 m × 3 m

beats.say: The plan: find the whole wall, then take away every opening that gets no paint. How many openings are there?

ask.ifNot: Count them: a window, another window, and a door. Each one is a piece of wall that gets no paint.

beats.say: The whole wall first. 10 times 4 is 40 square metres.
One window is a square of side 1.5. 1 times 1.5 is 1.5, and half of 1.5 is 0.75. Together, 2.25 square metres.
That was 1 window, and there are 2 of them. What area do the two windows cover together?

ask.ifNot: Each window covers 2.25 square metres, and there are 2 of them. So we need 2 lots of 2.25.

beats.say: 2 times 2.25 is 4.5 square metres. Now the door: 2 times 3 is 6 square metres.
Altogether, the openings take 4.5 plus 6, which is 10.5 square metres.
So the paint goes on 40 minus 10.5. 40 minus 10 is 30, and another 0.5 off leaves 29.5 square metres.
The easy slip is to take away only 1 window, when the question says two. Another is to forget the door, which leaves 35.5.
List every opening, find each area, add them up, and take the total from the wall.
Arjun is tiling a kitchen floor, 12 metres long and 8 metres wide. Each square tile has a side of 2 metres. How many tiles cover the whole floor?

board.text: Floor 12 m × 8 m, square tiles of side 2 m

beats.say: Tiles cover a surface, so this is about area. The floor is 12 times 8, which is 96 square metres.
Now the tile. It is a square with a side of 2 metres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 2 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 2 times 2 is 4. So each tile covers 4 square metres.
The floor is 96 square metres and each tile covers 4. How do we find the number of tiles?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many tile areas fit into the floor area. So we divide area by area: 96 by 4, not by the side of the tile.

beats.say: 96 divided by 4. Half of 96 is 48, and half of 48 is 24. Arjun needs 24 tiles.
Check by picturing the tiles. 6 fit along the length, and 4 rows fit down the breadth. 6 times 4 is 24.
Did you notice 48 on the way? It is one of the choices. It comes from dividing by 2, the side of the tile, when we should divide by its area.
For tiling: floor area, divided by the area of 1 tile.
Priya's rangoli is a rectangle, 9 metres long and 5 metres wide. Each packet of coloured powder covers 3 square metres. How many packets fill the whole rangoli?

board.text: Rangoli 9 m × 5 m, 1 packet covers 3 sq. m

beats.say: Powder fills the space inside the rangoli. Which sum measures that space?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides only measures along the edges. The space inside is the area: 5 rows of 9 square metres.

beats.say: 9 times 5 is 45. The rangoli covers 45 square metres.
Each packet covers 3 of those square metres. So we need to know how many 3s there are in 45. That is a division.
30 divided by 3 is 10, and the 15 left over, divided by 3, is 5. So 45 divided by 3 is 15 packets.
Check: 15 packets, 3 square metres each. 15 times 3 is 45. The whole rangoli is filled, with nothing left over.
Don't stop at 45. That is how many square metres there are, not how many packets. And 14 comes from adding 9 and 5, which is not an area.
So: find the area, then divide by what 1 packet covers.
Sanjay's kite is a triangle with sides of 15, 20 and 25 centimetres, and his friend says one angle is 90 degrees. Cloth costs 2 rupees for each square centimetre. What does the cloth cost?
Let's test what the friend said. In a right-angled triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side.

board.text: Right angle test: short² + short² = longest²

beats.say: 15 times 15 is 225. 20 times 20 is 400. Add them: 625. And 25 times 25 is 625 as well. It matches, so the triangle really is right-angled.
The right angle sits between two of the sides. Those two are the base and the height. Which two are they?

ask.ifNot: The longest side, 25, always lies opposite the right angle, on a slant. The two shorter sides, 15 and 20, are the ones that meet at the square corner.

beats.say: 15 and 20. Now, a right-angled triangle is exactly half of a rectangle. So its area is half of base times height.
15 times 20 is 300. Half of 300 is 150. So the kite needs 150 square centimetres of cloth.
Each square centimetre costs 2 rupees. 150 times 2 is 300 rupees.
Notice that 300 turned up twice: first as the area of the whole rectangle, then as the cost. The slips here are forgetting to halve, and using the slanted side, 25, as a height.
Right-angled triangle: half of the two short sides multiplied together. Then area times price.
Amit's bracket is an isosceles triangle. The two equal sides are 13 centimetres each, and the base is 10 centimetres. We want its perimeter.

board.text: Isosceles triangle: equal sides 13 cm, base 10 cm

beats.say: First, what is a perimeter? It is the distance all the way round a shape. Imagine an ant walking along every side until it is back where it started.

board.text: Perimeter = distance all the way round

beats.say: Isosceles means two of the sides are equal. So what are the three sides of this triangle?

ask.ifNot: The question says the two equal sides are each 13 centimetres. So 13 appears twice, and the base, 10, appears once.

beats.say: 13, 13 and 10. A triangle has 3 sides, so we add 3 numbers, even though the question only printed 2 different ones.
13 plus 13 is 26. Then 26 plus 10 is 36.
So the perimeter is 36 centimetres. That is the length of metal strip Amit needs.
Two slips to avoid. Stopping at 26 leaves out the base. And 13 plus 10 is only 23, which forgets that there are two sides of 13.
For any perimeter: list every side, count them, then add them all.
Ananya's courtyard is a square of side 20 metres. Inside it she paints a triangle: its base is one whole side of the square, and its tip touches the opposite side.

board.text: Square of side 20 m, triangle inside (base 20 m)
Gold paint for the rest: ₹12 per sq. m. Cost = ?

beats.say: The rest of the square is painted gold, at 12 rupees for each square metre. So we need the gold area. Start with the square: 20 times 20 is 400 square metres.
Now the triangle. Its base is 20 metres, and its tip touches the opposite side of the square. So how tall is it?

ask.ifNot: The triangle reaches from one side of the square right across to the opposite side. That distance is the side of the square.

beats.say: Base 20, height 20. A triangle's area is half of base times height. Half of 400 is 200 square metres.
Look at the picture. The triangle takes up exactly half of the square. So the gold part is the other half: 400 minus 200 is 200 square metres.
Gold paint costs 12 rupees for each square metre. 2 times 12 is 24, so 200 times 12 is 2,400 rupees.
The trap: 4,800 is the price of painting the whole square gold. The triangle is not gold, so only half of that is needed.
A triangle with its base on one side of a rectangle and its tip on the opposite side is always half of the rectangle.
Ravi's father is painting a wall, 6 metres long and 4 metres high. A square window of side 1 metre is not painted. 1 can of paint covers 5 square metres. How many cans must he buy?

board.text: Wall 6 m × 4 m, square window of side 1 m
1 can covers 5 sq. m. How many cans?

beats.say: First we need an area. Which area gets painted?

ask.ifNot: No paint goes on the window. So the window's area comes off the wall's area.

beats.say: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the wall, 6 times 4 is 24 square metres.
Now the window. It is a square of side 1, so its area is 1 times 1, which is just 1 square metre.
Now take the window away from the wall. 24 minus 1 is 23 square metres.
Now the cans. Each one covers 5 square metres. 4 cans cover 20, and 5 cans cover 25.
The wall needs 23 square metres of paint. How many cans?

ask.ifNot: 4 cans cover only 20 square metres. That leaves 3 square metres of wall with no paint, and a shop will not sell part of a can.

beats.say: 5 cans. The last one will not be used up, but it is needed.
Watch for two slips. 23 is the area, not the number of cans. And 4 is what you get by ignoring the leftover, which leaves the wall unfinished.
So: area to paint, divided by what 1 can covers. If it does not divide exactly, buy 1 more.
